scenes.title: A timeout is the queue you give up on

items.q: How do you stop a slow tool from freezing an agent?
items.a: Give **every tool a timeout**: run it in a worker (thread or process), wait at most N seconds, then return an error result. Prefer the client library's own timeouts for network calls.
items.trap: Relying on the model to "notice" it's slow. The model only acts after your code returns.

items.q: Thread or process for a tool timeout?
items.a: A **thread** is simple and fine for I/O, but it can't be killed. A **process** can be terminated and isolates memory and crashes, at the cost of more overhead.
items.trap: Claiming a thread timeout stops the work. It only stops the waiting.

scenes.question: After a thread timeout fires, what happens to the stuck tool?
options: It keeps running in the background; we just stop waiting
scenes.explain: Threads can't be killed from outside in Python. Use a separate process when you must be able to stop the work.

items.text: Every tool gets a timeout: never wait forever
A worker thread plus join(seconds) stops the waiting
Timeouts, missing items and bad input all become tool errors
Threads can't be killed: use processes for real isolation

captions.text: Real tools talk to the outside world: a database, a calendar service, a website.
And the outside world is sometimes slow, and sometimes doesn't answer at all.
In this lesson you'll make sure one stuck tool can never freeze your whole agent.
You'll explain why every tool needs a timeout.
Run a function with a timeout, using a thread.
Turn timeouts and other failures into tool errors.
And know the limits of thread timeouts.
Why do we need timeouts?
Think of standing in a queue at an office.
If nothing moves for an hour, at some point you decide to leave, and come back
another day.
You don't wait there forever.
A timeout is that decision, made in advance.
Wait at most, say, two seconds.
Then move on, with a clear message.
Without a timeout, one tool that never answers means the agent never answers, the
user waits forever, and in a server, that request holds resources until something
crashes.
Here's the idea in its simplest form.
We run the tool in a separate thread.
A thread is a second worker inside the same program, so our main code can keep an
eye on the clock.
Join with a number of seconds means: wait for the worker to finish, but no longer
than this.
If the worker is still running after that, we give up, and return a clear error
message instead of waiting forever.
A quick tool finishes in time, so we get its normal result.
This tool sleeps for sixty seconds, like a server that never answers.
After two seconds, we stop waiting, and get a timeout error.
And the total wait was two seconds, not sixty-two.
The agent stays responsive.
The project's version adds one important thing.
The worker stores either the result, or any exception the tool raised.
The thread is a daemon.
That means a stuck worker never stops the program from exiting.
After the wait, if it's still alive, we raise a tool error naming the tool and the
limit.
If the tool raised an error, we raise it again here, in the main thread, so it's
handled like any other error.
Otherwise we return the result.
And here's the function every tool call goes through.
First: does the tool exist?
Then: is the input valid, from lesson three.
And is the call allowed, which is next lesson.
Then: run the tool, with its own timeout.
And a lookup error, like a task that doesn't exist, becomes a tool error too.
Every problem ends up as a message, never a crash.
Let's see what the model receives in each case.
The tool finished: the normal result.
The tool was too slow: search notes timed out after two seconds, marked as an error.
The task doesn't exist: there is no task nine.
And bad input: the validation message from lesson three.
Here's the real agent.
This environment variable makes search notes sleep for thirty seconds, to play a
slow service.
Its timeout is two seconds.
After two seconds the agent gets a timeout observation, and finishes normally,
instead of hanging.
Let's be honest about the limits.
A thread timeout can stop waiting after N seconds, keep the agent responsive, and
report a clear error.
But it can't kill the stuck thread.
In Python, a thread can't be stopped from outside, so it keeps running in the
background.
It can't undo half-finished work.
And it can't protect you from a tool that uses huge amounts of memory.
For real isolation, run risky tools in a separate process, or a container.
And for network calls, use the library's own timeout too, like the SDK's timeout
setting from Module 2.

One.
List tasks, which reads a small local file.
Two.

Three.
Export report, which builds a PDF that usually takes about twenty seconds.
There's no single right number, but here's the reasoning.
A local file should take milliseconds, so a few seconds is generous.
A remote service: a few seconds, so a slow network doesn't freeze the agent.
A twenty-second job needs more, perhaps sixty seconds, or better, run it in the
background and let the agent check on it later.
Interview corner.
How do you stop a slow tool from freezing an agent?
Give every tool a timeout.
Run it in a worker, a thread or a process, wait at most N seconds, and then return
an error result.
For network calls, also use the library's own timeout.
The trap: expecting the model to notice it's slow.
The model can only act after your code returns.
Follow-up: would you use a thread or a process?
A thread is simple, and fine for waiting on input and output, but it can't be
killed.
A process can be terminated, and it isolates memory and crashes, but it costs more
to start.
The trap: claiming a thread timeout stops the work.
It only stops the waiting.
Quick check.
After a thread timeout fires, what happens to the stuck tool?
It keeps running in the background.
We just stop waiting for it.
If you must be able to stop the work, use a separate process.
Recap.
Every tool gets a timeout, so the agent never waits forever.
A worker thread, plus join with seconds, stops the waiting.
Timeouts, missing items and bad input all become tool errors.
And threads can't be killed, so use processes for real isolation.
Next lesson: the most important safety feature of all.
Permissions, and asking a human before anything dangerous happens.
